2d9b57464fff.tip: In combustion calorimetry, use the water's mass in mcΔT, but the burned fuel's mass change (initial minus final) for moles.
2d9b57464fff.why: Two different masses appear; mixing them up gives a wrong molar enthalpy even with the right sign.

be365d99870e.tip: Open-flame experiments give a less exothermic ΔH than the data-book value, because heat escapes, combustion is incomplete, or fuel evaporates.
be365d99870e.why: Evaluation parts ask why experiment and literature differ; heat loss shrinks ΔT, so the magnitude comes out too small.

2d4d9cb087ad.tip: Check your answer by closing the loop: formation enthalpy should equal the sum of all other steps taken the one way round.
2d4d9cb087ad.why: A cycle that does not close exposes a missed term or sign slip before you commit to an option.

5b59b92c1bb7.tip: If your lattice value looks unreasonable, first hunt for a missing second ionization or electron affinity term, then for a wrong sign.
5b59b92c1bb7.why: These are the commonest slips, so checking them first ruins fewer minutes than redoing everything.

b9d08e13f252.tip: A diatomic element's atomization step is half its bond enthalpy per mole of atoms. Two Cl atoms in the formula use one whole Cl–Cl bond.
b9d08e13f252.why: Explains why chlorine terms are given as halves or whole values, so you can match labelled arrows to the formula.
